# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Sudden cardiac death (SCD) due to ventricular arrhythmias remains a major cause of mortality worldwide. The transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (TV-ICD) has been the cornerstone of therapy for both primary and secondary prevention [1]. However, lead-related complications—including infection, venous occlusion, and lead fracture—drive substantial long-term morbidity [2,3]. The entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to avoid intravascular and intracardiac hardware, thereby eliminating lead-associated vascular complications [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, evidence, indications, and limitations of the S-ICD.

## Device Design and Rationale

The S-ICD comprises a pulse generator implanted in the left lateral thoracic region and a single parasternal subcutaneous electrode [4]. Unlike TV-ICDs, the S-ICD does not provide long-term bradycardia pacing, antitachycardia pacing (ATP), or cardiac resynchronization therapy [5]. It delivers an 80-J shock and offers transient post-shock pacing only [6]. The initial proof-of-concept studies demonstrated that subcutaneous defibrillation was feasible and that appropriate shock vectors could reliably terminate induced ventricular fibrillation [4]. Screening with surface electrocardiographic templates is required pre-implantation to ensure acceptable sensing and minimize T-wave oversensing [7].

## Clinical Efficacy Evidence

Early experience from the IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry established the safety and effectiveness of the S-ICD in converting both induced and spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias [6,8]. Pooled analyses confirmed high conversion rates exceeding 98% for discrete episodes [9]. The landmark PRAETORIAN trial was the first randomized comparison of the S-ICD versus TV-ICD in patients without pacing indications [10]. It demonstrated noninferiority of the S-ICD with respect to the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [10]. Lead-related complications were notably reduced, while the S-ICD group experienced more non-lead complications, balancing the overall outcome [10].

The UNTOUCHED study specifically evaluated inappropriate shock rates using contemporary programming with high rate cutoffs and demonstrated a low 18-month inappropriate shock rate, comparable to or better than historical TV-ICD data [11]. SMART Pass filtering and dual-zone programming substantially reduced T-wave oversensing and inappropriate therapies [12,13].

## Patient Selection

The S-ICD is particularly attractive in young patients, those with channelopathies (e.g., long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and patients at high infection risk such as those on hemodialysis [14,15]. Guidelines from professional societies endorse the S-ICD as an alternative to TV-ICD in patients without indications for bradycardia pacing, ATP, or resynchronization [16,17]. It is also valuable for patients with limited or compromised vascular access and those with prior device infections requiring reimplantation [18]. Careful electrocardiographic screening remains essential, as a proportion of candidates fail screening due to QRS/T-wave morphology, particularly in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy [19].

## Complications and Limitations

The principal limitation of the S-ICD is its inability to provide ATP, which can painlessly terminate monomorphic ventricular tachycardia [5]. Patients with recurrent monomorphic VT or those who may benefit from pacing are generally better served by a TV-ICD [16]. Inappropriate shocks, historically driven by T-wave oversensing and supraventricular arrhythmias, remain a concern though substantially mitigated by improved sensing algorithms [12,13,20]. Device-related infections still occur, though pocket infections rarely necessitate the complex lead extraction associated with TV-ICDs [21]. The larger generator and more extensive surgical pocket can lead to discomfort and erosion in thin patients [22].

## Emerging Developments

The combination of the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker offers a fully extravascular solution incorporating ATP capability, an area of active investigation [23,24]. The MODULAR ATP study evaluated communication between a leadless pacemaker and the S-ICD to deliver ATP [25]. Additionally, the extravascular ICD (EV-ICD), which positions the lead in the substernal space, allows pacing and ATP while avoiding the vasculature, representing a complementary technology [26,27]. Optimized two-incision implantation techniques and intermuscular generator placement have improved cosmetic and complication outcomes [28]. Long-term registry data continue to support durable performance and battery longevity [29]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest the S-ICD is reasonable in appropriately selected patients given reductions in lead-related reinterventions [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD is an established, effective alternative to the TV-ICD for patients requiring defibrillation without pacing needs. Randomized evidence from PRAETORIAN confirms noninferior safety and efficacy, with a favorable lead-complication profile [10]. Refinements in sensing algorithms and screening have reduced inappropriate shocks, while integration with leadless pacing and extravascular technologies promises to broaden applicability. Appropriate patient selection remains the key determinant of optimal outcomes.
